nremt-aemt-readiness-check-pharm-014.prompt: How is an oropharyngeal airway (OPA) correctly sized for an adult?

options.a: From the tip of the nose to the earlobe
options.b: By matching the width of the patient's little finger
options.c: From the center of the lips to the sternal notch
options.d: From the corner of the mouth to the earlobe or angle of the jaw

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-pharm-014.explanation: An OPA is measured from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe (or angle of the jaw). Too long can push the epiglottis over the glottis; too short can push the tongue back into the airway.

distractorExplanations.a: Nose-tip-to-earlobe is the sizing method for a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA), not an OPA.
distractorExplanations.c: The sternal notch is not a landmark for any basic airway adjunct.
distractorExplanations.b: Little-finger width is an old rule of thumb for NPA diameter, not OPA length.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-008.prompt: In START triage at a mass-casualty incident, an adult who is still not breathing after the airway is repositioned should be tagged:

options.a: Immediate (red)
options.b: Delayed (yellow)
options.c: Minor (green)
options.d: Expectant / deceased (black)

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-airway-008.explanation: In START, an apneic adult gets one airway repositioning. If breathing does not resume, the patient is tagged expectant/deceased so resources go to salvageable patients.

distractorExplanations.a: Immediate is for patients who begin breathing after repositioning or have RR over 30, delayed cap refill, or cannot follow commands.
distractorExplanations.b: Delayed is for patients who breathe, have adequate perfusion and mental status, but cannot walk.
distractorExplanations.c: Minor (green) is for the walking wounded, not an apneic patient.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-001.prompt: On arrival at a motor-vehicle crash, what is the AEMT's first priority?

options.a: Start the primary survey on the most injured patient
options.b: Size up the scene for hazards and ensure scene safety
options.c: Request additional units before leaving the ambulance
options.d: Determine the mechanism of injury from bystanders

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-001.explanation: Scene size-up starts with scene safety (traffic, fuel, electrical hazards, violence) and PPE. An injured rescuer cannot help anyone; patient care begins only when the scene is safe.

distractorExplanations.a: The primary survey comes after the scene is confirmed safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Mechanism of injury is assessed during size-up, after safety is addressed.
distractorExplanations.c: Requesting resources is part of size-up, but hazards and safety come first.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-002.prompt: A diabetic patient has deep, rapid respirations, a fruity breath odor, dry skin, and several days of heavy urination. This presentation most suggests:

options.a: Acute hypoglycemia from a missed meal
options.b: Hyperventilation from an anxiety attack
options.c: Alcohol intoxication with dehydration
options.d: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-002.explanation: Kussmaul respirations, fruity (ketone) breath, polyuria, and dehydration developing over days are classic DKA. Hypoglycemia has a rapid onset with cool, clammy skin.

distractorExplanations.a: Hypoglycemia comes on quickly with pale, sweaty skin and altered mental status, not days of polyuria.
distractorExplanations.c: Alcohol can mimic an odor on the breath, but it does not explain days of polyuria and Kussmaul breathing in a diabetic.
distractorExplanations.b: Anxiety hyperventilation does not cause ketone breath or days of heavy urination.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-003.prompt: During an active generalized tonic-clonic seizure, the AEMT should:

options.a: Hold the patient's limbs firmly to stop the movements
options.b: Protect the patient from injury, then manage the airway after the seizure
options.c: Place a bite block between the teeth to protect the tongue
options.d: Give oral glucose immediately to stop the seizure

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-003.explanation: Move hazards away, protect the head, and time the seizure. Do not restrain or put anything in the mouth. After the seizure, position the patient, suction, and support ventilation and oxygenation as needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Restraining a seizing patient can cause fractures and soft-tissue injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Nothing should be given by mouth to a patient who is seizing or cannot protect the airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Objects in the mouth can break teeth, cause airway obstruction, or injure the rescuer.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-004.prompt: The usual adult sublingual dose of nitroglycerin for suspected cardiac chest pain (per protocol) is:

options.a: 0.04 mg sublingual, repeated every minute
options.b: 4 mg sublingual as a single dose
options.c: 0.4 mg sublingual, repeatable about every 5 minutes
options.d: 40 mg intramuscular in the deltoid

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-004.explanation: Nitroglycerin is typically 0.4 mg SL (tablet or spray), repeated every 3–5 minutes up to protocol maximum (often 3 doses) while blood pressure remains adequate.

distractorExplanations.a: 0.04 mg is a tenfold underdose, and one-minute repeats would not allow blood pressure reassessment.
distractorExplanations.b: 4 mg is a tenfold overdose and could cause profound hypotension.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitroglycerin is not given intramuscularly by EMS.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-006.prompt: For suspected acute coronary syndrome with no contraindications, aspirin is typically given as:

options.a: 1 g dissolved under the tongue every hour
options.b: 81 mg swallowed whole with a full glass of water
options.c: 650 mg given slowly through an IV line
options.d: 160–325 mg chewed (often four 81 mg tablets)

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-006.explanation: Chewing non-enteric-coated aspirin (160–325 mg, commonly 324 mg as four 81 mg tablets) speeds absorption and platelet inhibition in suspected ACS.

distractorExplanations.b: A single 81 mg tablet swallowed whole is a low maintenance dose and absorbs more slowly.
distractorExplanations.c: EMS aspirin is given by mouth; IV aspirin is not in the AEMT formulary.
distractorExplanations.a: Hourly 1 g doses are an overdose and not how aspirin is given.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-008.prompt: Naloxone reverses opioid overdose because it:

options.a: Blocks opioid receptors and displaces the opioid
options.b: Stimulates beta-2 receptors to open the airways
options.c: Reverses benzodiazepines at the GABA receptor
options.d: Raises blood glucose by releasing liver glycogen

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-008.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive opioid-receptor antagonist. It displaces opioids and reverses respiratory depression; titrate to adequate breathing and support ventilation first with a BVM.

distractorExplanations.c: Benzodiazepine reversal is flumazenil, which is not an AEMT medication.
distractorExplanations.d: Releasing liver glycogen is how glucagon works.
distractorExplanations.b: Beta-2 stimulation describes albuterol, not naloxone.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-010.prompt: For adult anaphylaxis, intramuscular epinephrine is typically given as:

options.a: 1 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration as a rapid IV push
options.b: 0.3–0.5 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration into the lateral thigh
options.c: 3–5 mg of the 1 mg/mL concentration under the tongue
options.d: 0.03 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration into the deltoid

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-010.explanation: Adult IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis is 0.3–0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL (formerly 1:1,000), usually in the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated per protocol if symptoms persist.

distractorExplanations.c: Epinephrine is not given sublingually, and 3–5 mg is a dangerous overdose.
distractorExplanations.d: 0.03 mg is a tenfold underdose for an adult.
distractorExplanations.a: 1 mg IV push of 0.1 mg/mL is the cardiac-arrest dose, not anaphylaxis care with a pulse.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-014.prompt: An unresponsive adult has a blood glucose of 38 mg/dL and a patent IV. Per typical AEMT protocol, the preferred treatment is:

options.a: Oral glucose paste placed between cheek and gum
options.b: Subcutaneous insulin to stabilize glucose
options.c: IV dextrose (for example D10 or D50) per protocol
options.d: Oxygen only, then recheck glucose in 15 minutes

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-014.explanation: With IV access, dextrose (D10 titrated or D50 per protocol) corrects severe hypoglycemia fastest. Recheck glucose and mental status after administration.

distractorExplanations.a: Oral glucose needs an intact gag reflex and the ability to swallow; this patient is unresponsive.
distractorExplanations.b: Insulin lowers glucose further and is not an AEMT medication.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxygen does not treat hypoglycemia, and waiting risks brain injury.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-015.prompt: Glucagon is most useful for a hypoglycemic patient when:

options.a: The patient has no liver glycogen stores at all
options.b: The patient is alert and able to drink juice safely
options.c: The glucose is high and must be lowered quickly
options.d: IV access cannot be obtained, giving it IM or intranasally

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-trauma-015.explanation: Glucagon (IM or intranasal) releases stored liver glycogen as glucose. It is the fallback when IV dextrose is not possible. It works poorly when glycogen is depleted, for example in chronic alcoholism or malnutrition.

distractorExplanations.b: An alert patient who can swallow should get oral glucose or food.
distractorExplanations.c: Glucagon raises glucose; it is never used to lower it.
distractorExplanations.a: Without glycogen stores, glucagon has little or no effect.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-011.prompt: Inhaled albuterol relieves an asthma attack mainly by:

options.a: Blocking beta-1 receptors to slow the heart
options.b: Stimulating beta-2 receptors to relax bronchial smooth muscle
options.c: Reducing airway inflammation over the next several hours
options.d: Thinning mucus so it can be coughed up more easily

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-011.explanation: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist. It relaxes bronchial smooth muscle within minutes; expected side effects include tachycardia, tremor, and anxiety.

distractorExplanations.a: Beta-1 blockade describes beta blockers; albuterol usually raises heart rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Slow anti-inflammatory action describes corticosteroids.
distractorExplanations.d: Mucolytics thin secretions; albuterol is a bronchodilator.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-012.prompt: For an adult with hemorrhagic shock from uncontrolled internal bleeding, isotonic IV fluid is typically titrated to:

options.a: Restore a normal systolic pressure of about 120 mmHg
options.b: Run wide open until the patient's lungs sound wet
options.c: Give exactly 3 liters before any reassessment
options.d: Maintain minimal perfusion, such as a radial pulse or SBP near 80–90

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-012.explanation: Permissive hypotension limits fluid to what keeps minimal perfusion (for example a radial pulse or SBP about 80–90 mmHg per protocol). Raising pressure to normal can dislodge clots and dilute clotting factors.

distractorExplanations.a: Pushing to normal pressure can worsen internal bleeding before surgical control.
distractorExplanations.b: Fluid overload causes pulmonary edema and hemodilution.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixed large volumes without reassessment are not recommended.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-013.prompt: Before giving any medication, the AEMT checks the core "rights" of administration, which are:

options.a: Right diagnosis, hospital, insurance, and family consent
options.b: Right patient, drug, dose, route, and time, then document
options.c: Right vehicle, crew, radio channel, and destination
options.d: Right price, manufacturer, packaging, and storage shelf

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-013.explanation: The core rights are patient, medication, dose, route, and time, plus documentation. Also check expiration, clarity, and allergies before administering.

distractorExplanations.c: These are operational details, not medication rights.
distractorExplanations.d: Price and shelf location do not protect the patient from medication errors.
distractorExplanations.a: Diagnosis and insurance are not medication-safety checks.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-014.prompt: When peripheral IV access fails in a critically ill adult, which route gives the fastest reliable vascular access for fluids and medications?

options.a: Intramuscular injection into the deltoid
options.b: Subcutaneous infusion in the abdomen
options.c: Sublingual placement of oral medications
options.d: Intraosseous (IO) access, such as the proximal tibia or humerus

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-014.explanation: IO access reaches the non-collapsible marrow venous network and delivers fluids and drugs about as fast as IV. It is the standard backup when IV access fails in critical patients.

distractorExplanations.a: IM absorption is slower and unreliable in shock, and fluids cannot be infused IM.
distractorExplanations.c: Sublingual works for a few drugs only, not fluids or most emergency medications.
distractorExplanations.b: Subcutaneous absorption is slow and poor when perfusion is low.

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-015.prompt: In anaphylaxis, epinephrine's alpha-1 effect helps mainly by:

options.a: Relaxing bronchial smooth muscle to relieve wheezing
options.b: Constricting blood vessels to raise blood pressure and reduce swelling
options.c: Slowing the heart rate so the ventricles fill better
options.d: Blocking histamine receptors to stop the itching

nremt-aemt-readiness-check-medical-015.explanation: Alpha-1 stimulation causes vasoconstriction, which raises blood pressure and reduces mucosal edema. Beta-2 effects relax bronchial smooth muscle, and beta-1 effects increase heart rate and contractility.

distractorExplanations.a: Bronchodilation is a beta-2 effect of epinephrine.
distractorExplanations.d: Histamine blockade describes antihistamines such as diphenhydramine.
distractorExplanations.c: Epinephrine increases heart rate (beta-1); it does not slow it.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-001.prompt: When scheduling a patient who needs a fasting lipid panel, the medical assistant should:

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-006.prompt: When verifying insurance eligibility, the medical assistant should typically confirm:

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-008.prompt: On the AMT RMA, which telephone triage action is appropriate for a medical assistant? Select the best answer.

amt-rma-readiness-check-admin-015.prompt: Which scheduling method books several patients at the start of each hour and sees them in the order they arrive?

options.a: Stream scheduling
options.b: Wave scheduling
options.c: Open-hours scheduling
options.d: Cluster scheduling

amt-rma-readiness-check-admin-015.explanation: Wave scheduling books a group of patients at the top of the hour and sees them in arrival order, so late arrivals do not derail the day. Modified wave staggers some patients later in the hour.

distractorExplanations.a: Stream scheduling gives each patient an individual appointment time.
distractorExplanations.c: Open hours means no appointments; patients walk in during set hours.
distractorExplanations.d: Clustering groups similar procedures together, not several patients at the top of each hour.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-011.prompt: Following the CLSI order of draw for evacuated tubes, which is collected first?

options.a: Lavender-top (EDTA) tube
options.b: Gray-top (sodium fluoride) tube
options.c: Blood culture bottles or sterile tubes
options.d: Green-top (heparin) tube

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-011.explanation: CLSI order: blood cultures/sterile, light blue (citrate), red or gold (serum), green (heparin), lavender (EDTA), gray (fluoride/oxalate). Drawing sterile specimens first prevents contamination and additive carryover.

distractorExplanations.a: EDTA comes near the end; drawn early, its carryover can falsely raise potassium and lower calcium in later tubes.
distractorExplanations.b: Gray-top fluoride tubes are drawn last.
distractorExplanations.d: Heparin tubes are drawn after citrate and serum tubes, not first.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-012.prompt: For an accurate adult blood pressure, the cuff's inflatable bladder should encircle about:

options.a: 25% of the upper-arm circumference
options.b: 50% of the upper-arm circumference
options.c: 150% of the upper-arm circumference
options.d: 80% of the upper-arm circumference

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-012.explanation: The bladder length should encircle about 80% of the arm, with width about 40% of arm circumference. A cuff that is too small reads falsely high; one that is too large reads falsely low.

distractorExplanations.a: A bladder this small is undersized and gives falsely high readings.
distractorExplanations.b: Half the circumference is still too small for an accurate reading.
distractorExplanations.c: A bladder longer than the arm cannot be applied correctly and tends to read low.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-013.prompt: Where is the V1 electrode placed for a 12-lead ECG?

options.a: Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
options.b: Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
options.c: Fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line
options.d: Fifth intercostal space, left anterior axillary line

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-013.explanation: V1 goes at the 4th intercostal space just right of the sternum and V2 at the 4th intercostal space just left. V4 is at the 5th intercostal space midclavicular, and V3 is between V2 and V4.

distractorExplanations.a: The 4th intercostal space at the left sternal border is V2.
distractorExplanations.d: The anterior axillary line at V4's level is V5.
distractorExplanations.c: The 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line is V4.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-014.prompt: A standard steam autoclave cycle for wrapped instruments typically runs at about:

options.a: 100°C (212°F) at normal pressure for 5 minutes
options.b: 70°C (158°F) with alcohol vapor for 10 minutes
options.c: 121°C (250°F) at about 15 psi for 15–30 minutes
options.d: 60°C (140°F) in a dishwasher cycle for an hour

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-014.explanation: Gravity steam sterilization typically uses 121°C (250°F) at about 15 psi for 15–30 minutes depending on the load and wrapping. Follow the manufacturer's cycle and verify it with indicators.

distractorExplanations.a: Boiling at normal pressure does not reliably kill bacterial spores.
distractorExplanations.d: Dishwasher temperatures only sanitize; they do not sterilize.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol is a disinfectant, not a sterilizing method for instruments.

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-015.prompt: Intramuscular injections are given with the needle at an angle of:

options.a: 10–15 degrees
options.b: 45 degrees
options.c: 25–30 degrees
options.d: 90 degrees

amt-rma-readiness-check-clinical-015.explanation: IM injections are given at 90° to reach muscle tissue. Subcutaneous injections are usually at 45° (or 90° with short needles), and intradermal injections at 10–15°.

distractorExplanations.a: 10–15° is the intradermal angle, used for example for TB skin tests.
distractorExplanations.b: 45° is typical for subcutaneous injections.
distractorExplanations.c: About 15–30° is used for venipuncture, not IM injections.

amt-rma-readiness-check-admin-012.prompt: When is an alcohol-based hand rub NOT sufficient, so hands must be washed with soap and water?

options.a: Before touching a patient for a routine exam
options.b: After removing gloves when hands look clean
options.c: Before entering a clean supply room
options.d: When hands are visibly soiled or after C. difficile exposure

amt-rma-readiness-check-admin-012.explanation: Soap and water are required when hands are visibly soiled and after caring for patients with spore-forming organisms such as C. difficile, because alcohol does not kill spores.

distractorExplanations.a: Alcohol rub is appropriate before routine patient contact when hands are not soiled.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol rub is acceptable after glove removal if hands are not visibly soiled.
distractorExplanations.c: Alcohol rub is fine before entering a clean supply area.

amt-rma-readiness-check-admin-013.prompt: The main purpose of a clean-catch midstream urine collection is to:

options.a: Measure the total urine volume over 24 hours
options.b: Let the patient avoid cleansing before collection
options.c: Collect the most concentrated first-morning urine
options.d: Minimize contamination from skin and genital flora

amt-rma-readiness-check-admin-013.explanation: Cleansing the urethral area and collecting midstream urine reduces contamination from skin and genital flora, which matters for urine cultures.

distractorExplanations.a: Total volume requires a timed 24-hour collection.
distractorExplanations.c: First-morning specimens are about concentration, not contamination control.
distractorExplanations.b: Cleansing is a required step of a clean catch.

amt-rma-readiness-check-admin-014.prompt: For an adult capillary (fingerstick) puncture, the preferred site is:

options.a: The center tip of the index finger
options.b: The side of the thumb near the nail
options.c: The medial or lateral plantar heel surface
options.d: The palmar surface of the middle or ring finger, slightly off-center

amt-rma-readiness-check-admin-014.explanation: Use the fleshy palmar surface of the middle or ring finger, off-center and perpendicular to the fingerprint lines, and wipe away the first drop.

distractorExplanations.a: The index fingertip is more sensitive and callused; the center tip is near bone.
distractorExplanations.b: The thumb has a pulse and thicker tissue and is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.c: Heel sticks are used for infants, not adults.

options.a: A heart rate faster than 100 beats per minute
options.b: An enlarged heart seen on a chest X-ray
options.c: An irregular rhythm with no visible P waves
options.d: A heart rate slower than 60 beats per minute

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-001.explanation: Brady- means slow and -cardia refers to the heart. In adults, bradycardia is a resting rate below 60 beats per minute.

distractorExplanations.a: A rate over 100 is tachycardia.
distractorExplanations.c: An irregular rhythm without P waves suggests atrial fibrillation.
distractorExplanations.b: An enlarged heart is cardiomegaly.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-002.prompt: Which heart chamber pumps oxygenated blood out to the body through the aorta?

options.a: Right atrium
options.b: Left ventricle
options.c: Left atrium
options.d: Right ventricle

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-002.explanation: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and systemic circulation, which is why its wall is the thickest of the four chambers.

distractorExplanations.a: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae.
distractorExplanations.c: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and passes it to the left ventricle.
distractorExplanations.d: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

options.a: Visual examination
options.b: Surgical incision into
options.c: Creation of an opening
options.d: Surgical removal

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-003.explanation: -ectomy means excision or surgical removal, as in appendectomy.

distractorExplanations.b: Incision into is -otomy, as in tracheotomy.
distractorExplanations.c: Creating an opening is -ostomy, as in colostomy.
distractorExplanations.a: Visual examination is -scopy, as in endoscopy.

options.a: Adrenal cortex
options.b: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets
options.c: Anterior pituitary gland
options.d: Thyroid follicular cells

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-004.explanation: Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin. Alpha cells in the same islets secrete glucagon.

distractorExplanations.a: The adrenal cortex produces cortisol, aldosterone, and androgens.
distractorExplanations.d: Thyroid follicular cells make T3 and T4.
distractorExplanations.c: The anterior pituitary produces hormones such as GH, TSH, and ACTH.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-005.prompt: The functional unit of the kidney that filters blood and forms urine is the:

options.a: Alveolus
options.b: Neuron
options.c: Nephron
options.d: Villus

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-005.explanation: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Each nephron includes a glomerulus for filtration and tubules for reabsorption and secretion.

distractorExplanations.b: The neuron is the functional cell of the nervous system.
distractorExplanations.d: Villi line the small intestine and absorb nutrients.
distractorExplanations.a: Alveoli are air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-006.prompt: Which anatomical plane divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions?

options.a: Sagittal plane
options.b: Midsagittal plane
options.c: Transverse plane
options.d: Frontal (coronal) plane

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-006.explanation: The frontal (coronal) plane runs side to side and separates the front of the body from the back.

distractorExplanations.a: A sagittal plane divides the body into left and right parts.
distractorExplanations.c: The transverse plane divides the body into upper and lower parts.
distractorExplanations.b: The midsagittal plane divides the body into equal left and right halves.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-007.prompt: The combining form "hepat/o" refers to the:

options.a: Kidney
options.b: Liver
options.c: Stomach
options.d: Spleen

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-007.explanation: Hepat/o means liver, as in hepatitis (liver inflammation) and hepatomegaly (enlarged liver).

distractorExplanations.a: Kidney is nephr/o or ren/o.
distractorExplanations.d: Spleen is splen/o.
distractorExplanations.c: Stomach is gastr/o.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-008.prompt: The medical term for inflammation of a joint is:

options.a: Arthralgia
options.b: Osteitis
options.c: Arthritis
options.d: Myositis

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-008.explanation: Arthr/o means joint and -itis means inflammation, so arthritis is joint inflammation.

distractorExplanations.a: Arthralgia means joint pain, not inflammation.
distractorExplanations.b: Osteitis is inflammation of bone.
distractorExplanations.d: Myositis is inflammation of muscle.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-009.prompt: Most absorption of nutrients from digested food takes place in the:

options.a: Stomach
options.b: Esophagus
options.c: Large intestine
options.d: Small intestine

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-009.explanation: The small intestine, with its villi and microvilli, absorbs most nutrients. The large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

distractorExplanations.a: The stomach mixes and begins digesting food but absorbs little besides some water, alcohol, and certain drugs.
distractorExplanations.c: The large intestine absorbs mainly water and electrolytes.
distractorExplanations.b: The esophagus only transports food to the stomach.

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-010.prompt: The antecubital fossa, a common venipuncture site, is located:

options.a: On the back of the hand
options.b: On the anterior surface of the elbow
options.c: On the inner wrist
options.d: Behind the knee

amt-rma-readiness-check-anatomy-010.explanation: The antecubital fossa is the front (anterior) surface of the elbow. The median cubital vein there is usually the first-choice vein for venipuncture.

distractorExplanations.a: Dorsal hand veins are an alternate site, not the antecubital fossa.
distractorExplanations.d: The area behind the knee is the popliteal fossa.
distractorExplanations.c: The inner wrist has arteries and nerves close to the surface and is avoided.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: What is the difference between cleaning and sanitizing a food-contact surface?

options.a: Cleaning kills all germs; sanitizing only makes the surface look shiny
options.b: Cleaning removes food and dirt; sanitizing reduces pathogens to safe levels
options.c: They mean the same thing and either step can be skipped
options.d: Sanitizing removes grease; cleaning is only needed once a week

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Cleaning removes food, dirt, and grease; sanitizing then reduces pathogens on the clean surface to safe levels. Sanitizer does not work well on a dirty surface, so clean first.

distractorExplanations.c: They are different steps and both are required for food-contact surfaces.
distractorExplanations.d: Cleaning is what removes grease, and it is needed after every use and every 4 hours.
distractorExplanations.a: Cleaning does not reliably kill pathogens; that is the purpose of sanitizing.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: What is the correct order of steps when washing items in a three-compartment sink?

options.a: Wash, sanitize, rinse, scrape, towel-dry
options.b: Scrape, wash, rinse, sanitize, air-dry
options.c: Rinse, sanitize, wash, scrape, air-dry
options.d: Sanitize, scrape, wash, rinse, towel-dry

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Scrape or pre-rinse, wash in detergent, rinse in clean water, sanitize for the required contact time, then air-dry. Rinsing before sanitizing removes detergent that would weaken the sanitizer.

distractorExplanations.a: Rinsing after sanitizing removes the sanitizer, and towel-drying can recontaminate items.
distractorExplanations.c: Sanitizing before washing puts sanitizer on a dirty surface, where it cannot work.
distractorExplanations.d: Sanitizing must be the last wet step, after washing and rinsing.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: How should a food handler check that a sanitizer solution is the right strength?

options.a: Smell it to make sure it is strong enough
options.b: Use a test kit made for that sanitizer
options.c: Add extra sanitizer so it is always strong enough
options.d: Look at the color of the water in the sink

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Use the test kit or strips made for that sanitizer, and check concentration regularly because it drops with use. Too weak will not reduce pathogens; too strong can be unsafe.

distractorExplanations.a: Smell cannot measure concentration and exposes the handler to fumes.
distractorExplanations.d: Water color does not show sanitizer strength.
distractorExplanations.c: Too much sanitizer can be toxic and leave harmful residue.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: Between uses, wet wiping cloths used on food-contact surfaces should be:

options.a: Kept in an apron pocket
options.b: Stored in a sanitizer solution
options.c: Left on the prep counter
options.d: Hung over a hot pan to dry

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Wet wiping cloths are kept in a sanitizer solution of the correct strength, and the solution is changed on schedule. Cloths for raw meat areas are kept separate.

distractorExplanations.c: A cloth left on the counter grows bacteria and can contaminate food.
distractorExplanations.d: Drying a cloth over cooking equipment is a fire and contamination risk.
distractorExplanations.a: A cloth in a pocket or apron spreads pathogens between surfaces.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: After cleaning and sanitizing, how should dishes and utensils be dried?

options.a: Wiped with a clean kitchen towel
options.b: Air-dried on a clean, sanitized rack
options.c: Dried with paper towels right away
options.d: Dried with a cloth from the wiping bucket

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Items should air-dry on a clean rack or drainboard. Towel-drying can put pathogens back on sanitized surfaces.

distractorExplanations.a: Towels can recontaminate sanitized items.
distractorExplanations.d: Wiping cloths are for surfaces, not for drying sanitized dishes.
distractorExplanations.c: Paper towels are not the approved drying method for sanitized ware.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: Before preparing an allergen-special order on shared equipment, the food handler should:

options.a: Wipe the equipment with a dry towel
options.b: Wash, rinse, and sanitize the equipment first
options.c: Rinse the equipment briefly under hot water
options.d: Use the same utensils as long as they look clean

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: To prevent allergen cross-contact, equipment, utensils, and surfaces must be washed, rinsed, and sanitized before use, or dedicated allergen-free equipment used. Handlers also wash hands and change gloves.

distractorExplanations.a: A dry towel spreads allergen residue instead of removing it.
distractorExplanations.c: A quick rinse does not remove allergen proteins.
distractorExplanations.d: Invisible allergen residue can still cause a severe reaction.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: Where should dirty mop water be dumped?

options.a: In the handwashing sink
options.b: In the food-prep sink
options.c: In the three-compartment sink
options.d: In a utility (service) sink

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Dirty mop water goes into a utility or service sink or a floor drain meant for that use. It must never go into handwashing, prep, or dishwashing sinks.

distractorExplanations.a: Handwashing sinks are for handwashing only.
distractorExplanations.b: Dumping dirty water where food is prepped contaminates the sink.
distractorExplanations.c: The three-compartment sink is for cleaning dishes and utensils.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: Which of these is an example of a physical contaminant?

options.a: Norovirus on a food handler's hands
options.b: Metal shavings from a worn can opener
options.c: Sanitizer sprayed near an open salad
options.d: Ciguatoxin in a large reef fish

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Physical contaminants are objects such as metal shavings, glass, staples, hair, or bandages. Keep can openers in good repair and inspect food for foreign objects.

distractorExplanations.a: Norovirus is a biological contaminant.
distractorExplanations.d: Ciguatoxin is a biological toxin.
distractorExplanations.c: Sanitizer is a chemical contaminant.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: Hepatitis A is most often spread in foodservice when:

options.a: Raw chicken is cooked to only 145°F
options.b: Canned food is stored past its best-by date
options.c: Cooked rice cools too slowly at room temperature
options.d: An infected handler with poor handwashing touches ready-to-eat food

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route, usually through ready-to-eat food handled by an infected worker with poor handwashing. Cooking does not help for food served raw, so handwashing, no bare-hand contact, and excluding ill staff are the controls.

distractorExplanations.a: Undercooked poultry is linked to Salmonella and Campylobacter, not hepatitis A.
distractorExplanations.c: Slow cooling of rice is linked to Bacillus cereus.
distractorExplanations.b: A best-by date is about quality, not hepatitis A transmission.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.prompt: In a walk-in cooler, how should raw poultry be stored relative to ready-to-eat food?

options.a: On the bottom shelf, below ready-to-eat food
options.b: On the same shelf, as long as items are wrapped
options.c: Anywhere, because the cooler keeps food at 41°F
options.d: On the top shelf so it stays coldest

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-cl.explanation: Store ready-to-eat food on top and raw items below in order of cooking temperature, with raw poultry (165°F) on the bottom. This keeps drips from contaminating food that will not be cooked.

distractorExplanations.b: Wrapping helps, but raw meat still goes below ready-to-eat food.
distractorExplanations.c: Cold temperatures slow growth but do not prevent cross-contamination.
distractorExplanations.d: Raw poultry on top can drip onto everything below it.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-co.prompt: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli is most commonly linked to:

options.a: Cooked rice left at room temperature
options.b: Undercooked ground beef and contaminated produce
options.c: Large predatory reef fish such as barracuda
options.d: Home-canned vegetables with bulging lids

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-co.explanation: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli comes from cattle intestines. It is linked to undercooked ground beef (cook to 155°F) and to produce contaminated by animal feces.

distractorExplanations.c: Large reef fish are associated with ciguatera toxin.
distractorExplanations.d: Bulging home-canned goods suggest Clostridium botulinum.
distractorExplanations.a: Rice left at room temperature is associated with Bacillus cereus.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-co.prompt: Why should acidic foods such as tomato sauce not be stored in copper or galvanized containers?

options.a: The containers make the sauce spoil faster from mold
options.b: The acid causes the food to reach unsafe temperatures
options.c: Metal can leach into the food and cause toxic-metal poisoning
options.d: These containers are too heavy to lift safely

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-co.explanation: Acidic foods can dissolve copper, zinc, lead, and similar metals into the food and cause chemical (toxic-metal) poisoning. Use food-grade containers only.

distractorExplanations.a: The main hazard is chemical leaching, not faster mold growth.
distractorExplanations.d: Weight is not the food safety issue.
distractorExplanations.b: Container material does not change the food's temperature.

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-co.prompt: A food handler cuts raw chicken, then slices bread for sandwiches without washing hands or changing the cutting board. This is an example of:

options.a: Time-temperature abuse
options.b: Physical contamination
options.c: Toxic-metal poisoning
options.d: Cross-contamination

servsafe-food-handler-readiness-check-co.explanation: Cross-contamination moves pathogens from raw food to ready-to-eat food by hands, boards, or utensils. Wash hands, change gloves, and clean and sanitize (or switch) boards between tasks.

distractorExplanations.a: Time-temperature abuse is leaving food in the danger zone too long.
distractorExplanations.b: Physical contamination involves foreign objects such as glass or metal.
distractorExplanations.c: Toxic-metal poisoning comes from food reacting with metal containers.
